item.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
item.description: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company. The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion. That kind of number was once unheard of for a company’s first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth — and most recently the AI boom — has changed that. Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars (following SpaceX just months ago), and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits. Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology’s risks overall. Here are some numbers to help understand Thursday’s IPO. The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of trading on Thursday, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June. The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix (US$26.5 billion in July) and oil giant Saudi Aramco (US$25.6 billion in 2019). Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion The initial price per share was set at US$83. But in early trading, that spiked more than 30 per cent — to US$111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon ET. By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That’s still over 17 per cent higher than its initial public offering price. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion. Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11 Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S&P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018. How far a trillion U.S. dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 93 million miles That would surpass the roughly 93 million miles (150 million kilometres) between Earth and the sun. The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million. There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the U.S. Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122. --- Wyatte Grantham-Philips, The Associated Press

item.title: Anthropic set to begin trading as a US$1.5-trillion company in the biggest IPO on record
item.description: Anthropic is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday after pricing its IPO at US$83 per share, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion and surpassing SpaceX as the largest ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened for trading Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods. Anthropic shares began trading at US$111.50, spiking more than 30 per cent above the initial public offering price, before closing at US$97.17, more than 17 per cent higher than the IPO. A day earlier, the company priced its IPO at US$83 per share, enough to value the entire business at US$1.5 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record. At the start of trading, the valuation leaped to US$2.01 trillion. The initial price was surprisingly high given that investor worries had ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI’s chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, in a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a much lower price range between US$70 to US$78 per share. “It’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia,” said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co. “The pricing shows strong demand among investors.” A big test remains if investors maintain the classic “IPO pop” by keeping the stock aloft in its first day — or if it will tumble by the close. The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool offered 980 million shares to the public, which at US$83 per share translated into proceeds of US$81 billion. Anthropic’s soaring debut on Wall Street was not enough to carry the rest of the market. U.S. stock indexes fell after a morning rally quickly evaporated. IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt In addition to market jitters over AI, the IPO is facing down a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. For its part, Anthropic rival OpenAI decided to postpone its initial offering until next year. The company, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, is also facing big financial challenges ahead. Anthropic already has taken on US$6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. While the company showed ample cash in its last financial report, it would have likely run through it quickly given its outsize spending plans. In the same financial report, the company said it had signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend US$900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including US$70 billion in the next 12 months. Such massive spending by AI companies, comparable to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads, have scared lenders, helping to push borrowing rates high recently. With the IPO, though, Anthropic will now have enormous resources to accelerate its expansion without taking on more debt. The offering will also allow its employees to sell vested stock, making many of them millionaires overnight — and potentially adding billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei. AI industry faces concerns about data centres, a possible bubble and regulations Founded five years ago by the siblings along with several other former OpenAI veterans, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector. Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months. In comments at the opening bell Thursday, Amodei sought to dampen fears by stressing a commitment to ensure humans are in control of the technology. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same,” he said. ”The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.” Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry as a backlash unfolds against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centres, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction. In his comments Thursday, Amodei also touted a range of positive uses for AI, noting that Claude already is helping scientists do quicker research and that the technology could help accelerate that progress in the future. “Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox and polio history for most of the world,” he said, “but progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families.” He also pointed to Claude’s use across companies, nonprofits and government services. “I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future,” he said. Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group. “Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said Tuesday in an interview with The Associated Press at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.” ___ Bernard Condon and Barbara Ortutay, The Associated Press Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

item.title: TD report examines financial health of Canadian households
item.description: As Canadians grapple with elevated rates of unemployment and inflation, as well as the fallout from an ongoing trade war with the U.S., a new report suggests most households are still finding ways to ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: As Canadians grapple with elevated rates of unemployment and inflation, as well as the fallout from an ongoing trade war with the U.S., a new report suggests most households are still finding ways to make ends meet, despite a number of troubling economic data points. “Canadian consumers are holding up reasonably well,” wrote Maria Solovieva, CFA and economist, in a report released Thursday by TD Economics. The report noted that real consumer spending grew at a nearly three per cent pace through the first half of 2026, suggesting Canadians have remained resilient in the face of numerous economic challenges. “But solid spending growth masks pockets of financial strain, particularly in Ontario,” Solovieva wrote. “A closer look at several indicators – insolvencies, delinquencies, and mortgage arrears – reveals a mixed picture, with some measures showing signs of stabilizing while others continue to deteriorate.” Weakness in Ontario In Canada’s largest province, the current financial strain on Canadians is “most visible,” according to the report. “Ontario stands out with mortgage arrears nearly tripling from pre-pandemic norms and approaching their Global Financial Crisis (GFC) peak. This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs,” it said. Mortgage arrears have also risen, to a lesser extent, in British Columbia, as both provinces experienced significant home price gains during the pandemic period, the report noted, leaving many homeowners with larger mortgage balances relative to income. While the pace of growth in B.C. mortgage arears has slowed more recently, the rate has continued to climb in Ontario, hitting 0.34 per cent in August. That’s nearly triple its pre-pandemic level of around 0.12 per cent and approaching the 0.43 per cent peak during the GFC, according to the report. “Still, perspective matters. Even at today’s elevated rate, roughly one in 300 Ontario mortgages is in arrears,” said Solovieva. “These missed payments do not necessarily translate into more severe financial distress or credit losses. Many borrowers retain substantial home equity, giving both households and lenders some flexibility to manage financial difficulties.” Those who are most vulnerable now are homeowners who purchased property during the 2021 and 2022 housing peak, when prices were highest and “equity cushions may be thinnest,” the report noted. Eyes on the labour market Across Canada, but particularly in Ontario, Canadians are faced with the combination of high living costs and a weakening labour market, which has hit some of the province’s traditional manufacturing centres hardest. “Notably, more than 35 per cent of people living in households in Oshawa, Windsor and Hamilton report difficulties meeting their financial needs – the highest among Canada’s largest cities,” wrote Solovieva. “Unemployment rates in all three cities are also above the national average, underscoring how labour market weakness is compounding existing affordability pressures in some regions.” At a national level, the labour market will continue to be a key indicator of the financial health of Canadians going forward, the report said. Earlier this month, Statistics Canada reported that the country’s unemployment rate rose to 6.7 per cent in October. It marked the third consecutive month of net job losses for the Canadian economy. ‘Little reason to sound the alarm’ TD says it expects stronger economic and labour market growth next year. However, forecasting accurately is difficult given the uncertainty surrounding Canada’s trading relationship with the U.S. as well as ongoing global conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. “Despite these vulnerabilities, we see little reason to sound the alarm bell over a broader deterioration in household credit performance. Ontario’s mortgage arrears are rising but are forecast to decline next year as the economy improves,” Solovieva argued. “If weak hiring gives way to widespread job losses… mortgage arrears could rise further and remain elevated for longer, but with stronger economic growth and a recovering labour market in our forecast, households in Ontario and across Canada are expected to bend but not break.”
